question: What has each of the five actually disclosed about advisor compensation structures?

claims.text: Morgan Stanley: In its 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025), the firm disclosed that for certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues. | It also disclosed that deferred compensation for financial advisors in the Wealth Management business segment is generally composed of 75% cash-based awards and 25% stock-based awards, and that its compensation and benefits expenses include base salaries and fixed allowances, formulaic programs, discretionary incentive compensation, amortization of deferred cash and equity awards, changes in the fair value of referenced notional DCP investments, carried interest, severance costs, and other items such as health and welfare benefits. | Employees (including financial advisors) are permitted to allocate deferred cash-based awards among a menu of notional investments selected by the firm (fixed income, equity, commodity and money market funds). | A Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor (MSVA) is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee, and the amount of the fee a client pays is a factor in calculating the Financial Advisor's compensation, giving the advisor a financial incentive not to reduce fees. | On the 4Q 2025 earnings call the firm said it will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation. | InvestmentNews (October 2026) reported Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, and that the firm has for years taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue as deferred compensation requiring years of vesting.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Schwab's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it offers a compensation package rewarding employee and company performance, encompassing base pay, performance-based incentive pay, equity awards, recognition awards, and health and wellness benefits. | It describes a noncontributory, unfunded, nonqualified financial consultant career achievement plan under which eligible financial consultants can receive earned cash payments after retirement contingent on performance levels, tenure, age, and client transitioning, with full vesting at age 60 and at least ten years of service. | The compensation of SWAI and SWAI Associates does not vary based on specific investment recommendations and is not tied to investment performance. | Financial Consultants may also receive compensation when clients purchase certain investments or products they recommend or introduce. | Schwab uses adjusted diluted EPS and return on tangible common equity as components of performance criteria for employee bonus and certain executive management incentive compensation arrangements. | Its 2022 Stock Incentive Plan provides for granting options and restricted stock units to employees and non-employee directors, and its deferred compensation plan for certain eligible employees permits deferral of certain cash compensation.

Edward Jones: Its 2025 10-K and ADV disclose that financial advisors are generally compensated on a commission basis, subject to a minimum guaranteed salary, and may be entitled to additional compensation based on branch office profitability and Partnership profitability. | Most financial advisors receive a portion of the Program Fee (at Edward Jones' discretion), while some receive a salary in addition to or in lieu of it; the fee rate paid is the same regardless of the model or advisory program. | The Program Fee, assets under care, and Reserve Line Advance balances impact most advisors' bonus eligibility and amount, and may impact eligibility for limited partnership profits interest. | Most advisors are eligible for the Travel Award Program based on new and existing assets under care. | Advisors typically earn more upfront in brokerage commissions but more over time in Advisory Solutions Fund Models, and may receive compensation on Reserve Line Advances depending on branch profitability. | The firm maintains a non-qualified deferred compensation plan for certain advisors, offers retiring advisors retirement transition plans, and notes a significant portion of successful advisors' compensation is variable based on Partnership profitability.

Merrill: Its 2026 ADV discloses that an Advisor earns compensation based on revenue Merrill earns from the Merrill Lynch Fee, other fees and costs, Sales Charges on brokerage account transactions, and referrals to Affiliates. | Advisors are eligible for a compensation award, payable over a defined period, from an incentive program based on meeting prior-year growth targets in new households and in assets and liabilities; an Advisor is subject to a reduction in their incentive compensation grid if they fail to achieve growth in the assets and liabilities component for two consecutive years. | Advisors do not receive additional compensation from advisory client assets held in the Cash Sweep Program. | Advisors joining from other firms generally receive payments (salary guarantees, upfront awards, deferred payments, recruitment loans) based largely on the size of their prior-firm business, conditioned on assets in accounts they service at Merrill. | Merrill's Advisor Development Program recruiting page discloses base salary and unlimited earning potential. | Elements of field management compensation are based on revenues to Merrill and on advisors meeting strategic goals. | Recommending Style Manager Strategies with no or lower Manager Fees can let an Advisor negotiate a higher Merrill Lynch Fee Rate.

Raymond James Financial: Its 10-K, ADV, and affiliation-options pages disclose that payouts to independent advisors are higher than to employee advisors because independents cover their own overhead (real estate, health insurance). | For the Traditional Employee model the payout is up to 50% with employee benefits; the Corporate RIA model discloses an 81% to 90% payout. | Employee advisors' compensation primarily includes a payout on revenues they generate plus participation in benefit plans, while independent contractors generally bear their own direct costs and receive a higher payout percentage. | An advisor can receive a higher portion of the fee as annual revenue generation rises; the Advisor Mastery Program salary declines each year as clients and revenues increase. | The firm offers transition assistance, bonuses, deferred compensation arrangements, enhanced pay-outs, repayable loans, and administrative fee reimbursements; it may grant RSUs on initial employment or in lieu of cash for bonuses above $275,000. | It reported a total compensation ratio of 65.7% and $2.58 billion of compensation expense for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, and a 64.8% ratio for the quarter ended March 31, 2025.

Morgan Stanley: Its 10-K states compensation for certain revenue-producing Wealth Management and Investment Management employees is largely paid on formulaic payouts linked to revenues. | The ADV discloses the fee amount a client pays is a factor in advisor compensation, and that below a certain fee-rate threshold the advisor gets credit for less than the total fee. | A Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor is paid a base salary plus discretionary bonus and retains no portion of the advisory fee. | InvestmentNews (October 2026) reported Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027.

Raymond James Financial: Its affiliation-options pages disclose payout rates by model: Traditional Employee up to 50% gross payout with benefits, Advisor Select 70-80% gross payout with benefits, Independent Contractor 81% to 90% payout, and Corporate RIA 81% to 90% payout. | Its 10-K states independent contractor advisors receive a higher payout percentage than employee advisors because they bear their own direct costs. | The CEO stated (1Q 2026) that even on the employee side the firm has tiered payout systems, so higher production moves an advisor up the payout grid. | The ADV discloses that an advisor's share of the fee rises with annual revenue generation.

Morgan Stanley: The ADV discloses a Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus. | The 10-K states deferred compensation for Wealth Management financial advisors is generally 75% cash-based awards and 25% stock-based awards (under programs generally containing vesting, clawback and cancellation provisions), and that compensation and benefits expenses include formulaic programs and discretionary incentive compensation.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Its 2025 10-K (Advisor Services segment) states the compensation package includes performance-based incentive pay and equity awards in addition to base pay, and that adjusted diluted EPS and return on tangible common equity are components of performance criteria for employee bonus and certain executive management incentive compensation.

Edward Jones: Its 10-K and ADV disclose that advisors may be entitled to additional bonus compensation based on branch and Partnership profitability; bonuses are determined by overall Partnership profitability and individual advisor performance. | The Program Fee, assets under care, and Reserve Line Advance balances impact most advisors' bonus eligibility and amount, and may impact eligibility for a limited partnership profits interest. | Most advisors are eligible for the Travel Award Program (travel or cash award in lieu) based on new and existing assets under care. | If Partnership profitability decreases, bonuses and profit-sharing may be decreased or eliminated.

Merrill: Its ADV discloses advisors are eligible for a compensation award from an incentive program based on prior-year growth targets in new households and assets/liabilities, and that an Advisor faces a reduction in the incentive compensation grid if they fail to achieve growth in the assets and liabilities component for two consecutive years. | Advisors joining from other firms receive recruitment payments (salary guarantees, upfront awards, deferred payments, recruitment loans) that are in addition to the incentive compensation to which they are otherwise entitled. | Field management compensation is based on revenues and on advisors meeting strategic goals including the assets/liabilities growth component.

Raymond James Financial: Its ADV discloses financial incentives for affiliating that include bonuses, transition assistance, deferred compensation arrangements, enhanced pay-outs, repayable loans, and administrative fee reimbursements, as well as recognition clubs that can yield paid travel, expense reimbursement, and deferred compensation awards. | The 10-K states competitive pay packages include base salary, incentive bonus, and equity compensation programs, and that RSUs may be granted in lieu of cash for a portion of the annual bonus to officers and certain other employees receiving an annual bonus over $275,000. | PCG recruiting and retention-related compensation includes cash and equity awards issued for recruiting, retention, or acquisitions.

Morgan Stanley: According to a FINRA arbitration award reported by InvestmentNews (November 2026), Morgan Stanley sought to claw back $2.46 million in recruiting bonus loans plus attorney's fees and interest from former advisor Sam Te Su, who had already paid back the loans before the hearing. Why it might matter: this is one instance of the firm's earlier practice of issuing recruiting bonus loans in the form of promissory notes that brokers pay back over time, as described in related trade-press reporting on a separate clawback against former advisor Darryl Cohen.

Morgan Stanley: InvestmentNews (August 2026) reported Morgan Stanley sought to claw back recruiting bonus money from former advisor Darryl Cohen via promissory notes (loans brokers pay back over time), and a FINRA arbitrator awarded Morgan Stanley $8.13 million in damages plus $561,000 in legal fees. Why it might matter: the award followed Cohen's March conviction for wire fraud and investment advisor fraud, and the firm's 2021 suit alleged breach of contract over the recruiting bonus promissory notes.

Morgan Stanley: InvestmentNews (October 2026) reported Morgan Stanley is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plan, and is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027. Why it might matter: the same reporting indicates retention bonuses had essentially replaced deferred compensation money for certain employee advisors who earlier became independent contractors or business owners, and that Morgan Stanley and Merrill are instead adhering to a more traditional approach.

Edward Jones: Its 2025 10-K discloses that eligible retiring financial advisors are offered individually tailored retirement transition plans compensating them for providing client transition services under a retirement and transition agreement that is generally for five years, with most participants paid ratably over four years. Why it might matter: these transition plans specifically compensate retiring advisors for successfully transitioning clients, which is a form of transition pay connected to succession rather than new-advisor recruiting.

Merrill: Its 2026 ADV discloses that advisors who join from other firms generally receive payments in connection with the move, in forms including salary guarantees, upfront awards, and compensation contingent on continued employment (deferred payments, recruitment loans), with amounts generally based to a large extent on the size of the business at their prior firm, and future payments conditioned on total assets in accounts they service at Merrill; these bonuses are additional to their otherwise-earned incentive compensation. Why it might matter: the disclosure notes these future asset-based payments create a conflict of interest because the Advisor has an incentive to recommend that clients transfer assets to Merrill.

Raymond James Financial: For the three months ended June 30, 2026, the firm reported PCG recruiting and retention-related compensation of $117 million. Why it might matter: the firm broke out this line to show the impact of recruiting costs, which rose 5% versus the prior quarter amid strong recruiting activity.

Raymond James Financial: For the three months ended March 31, 2026, the firm reported PCG recruiting and retention-related compensation of $111 million. Why it might matter: the firm broke out this line to provide transparency on recruiting and retention costs, which have increased as a direct result of strong recruiting activity.

Raymond James Financial: For the three months ended December 31, 2025, the firm reported PCG recruiting and retention-related compensation of $107 million. Why it might matter: this line item was newly introduced commencing that quarter to aid understanding of the impact of recruiting and retention costs, which the firm attributes to strong recruiting successes.

Raymond James Financial: The CFO stated (fiscal 2025) that adjusted compensation expense included amortization of transition assistance provided to recruited advisors and other retention awards to existing advisors in the aggregate amount of $355 million, up approximately 11% versus fiscal 2024. Why it might matter: the firm characterized these transition-assistance and retention costs as a direct result of strong recruiting, reflecting a component of investing in organic growth.

Raymond James Financial: The 10-K (year ended September 30, 2025) reported loans to financial advisors, net increased $300 million due to its recruiting activities. Why it might matter: these loans to newly recruited financial advisors are recruiting-related financing whose costs the firm elsewhere notes could adversely affect financial results.

Raymond James Financial: The firm defines PCG recruiting and retention-related compensation to include cash and equity awards issued for recruiting activities, retention of existing advisors, or acquisitions, expensed over a service period typically between 5 and 10 years. Why it might matter: this definitional disclosure was added as the firm began breaking out recruiting and retention costs to aid understanding of their impact on the business.

Raymond James Financial: The ADV discloses financial incentives for affiliating including transition assistance, bonuses, deferred compensation arrangements, enhanced pay-outs, repayable business transition or working capital loans, and administrative fee reimbursements. Why it might matter: these affiliation incentives are the mechanisms through which the firm extends loans and other recruiting-related benefits to newly recruited advisors.

Raymond James Financial: The 10-K states that within the financial services industry other firms offer guaranteed contracts, upfront payments, and increased compensation, and that Raymond James' financial results may be adversely affected by costs incurred for any loans or other incentives offered to newly recruited financial advisors. Why it might matter: the firm itself flags that these recruiting loans and incentives are a cost it bears to attract advisors, consistent with the $300 million increase in loans to financial advisors reported for fiscal 2025.

Raymond James Financial: For the three months ended September 30, 2024, the firm reported acquisition-related retention compensation expense of $9 million. Why it might matter: this retention award amortization is part of the broader pool of cash and equity retention awards the firm issues in connection with recruiting and acquisitions.

Morgan Stanley: On the 4Q 2025 earnings call, the firm announced it will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation, saying the change will reduce accounting-driven volatility and simplify its compensation program. Why it might matter: the firm stated these changes support its overall investment into its financial advisors, even though they carry some transitional costs.

Morgan Stanley: The firm disclosed it was transitioning, over the first quarter of 2026, all economic hedges for its Wealth Management deferred cash-based compensation (DCP) obligations to derivative instruments. Why it might matter: this change to how DCP obligations are hedged accompanies the increase in the cash component of advisor compensation and is intended to reduce accounting-driven volatility.

Morgan Stanley: InvestmentNews (October 2026) reported Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors must generate 10% more revenue to receive the same pay. Why it might matter: the same reporting notes the firm has for years taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue as deferred compensation requiring multi-year vesting, which the pay-threshold increase interacts with.

Merrill: In October 2026, Merrill executives stated the firm has returned to veteran broker recruiting with a more aggressive offer, after largely pulling back from veteran broker recruiting at the end of 2017; recruited assets to the wealth unit doubled year-over-year. Why it might matter: the return to a more aggressive recruiting offer followed Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf restoring a focus on hiring after taking over in 2023.

Raymond James Financial: Commencing the fiscal first quarter of 2026 (quarter ended December 31, 2025), the firm began presenting recruiting and retention-related compensation expense in the Private Client Group segment for each reporting period to aid understanding of the impact of such costs on the business. Why it might matter: the firm said these costs have increased as a direct result of strong recruiting successes and reflect a component of investing in organic growth, its highest capital-deployment priority.

Raymond James Financial: CEO Paul Shoukry said (4Q 2025) the firm would begin breaking out, starting the following quarter, the upfront money amortization that hits compensation expense in the Private Client Group business, citing its recruiting activity. Why it might matter: the CEO noted the firm's annual recruiting had reached roughly a medium-sized acquisition in scale ($400 million of prior-firm production recruited that year), motivating the added disclosure transparency.

Raymond James Financial: CEO Paul Shoukry said (1Q 2026) the firm has broken out the cost of recruiting and retention in its reporting, noting its annual recruiting is now equivalent to a medium-sized acquisition. Why it might matter: the CEO said the firm wanted to provide transparency so stakeholders could see exactly how much is being paid to recruit and grow the firm.

Comparison: The five firms differ materially in how much detail they disclose. Raymond James discloses the most granular public data: specific payout ranges by affiliation model (up to 50%, 70-80% gross, 81-90%), a tiered employee payout grid, a defined total compensation ratio with dollar figures, and a separately disclosed recruiting/retention compensation line with dollar amounts. Morgan Stanley discloses formulaic payout structure, the 75%/25% deferred-compensation mix, and a discrete bonus framework for its Virtual Advisor, but no percentage payout grid. Edward Jones describes a commission-plus-minimum-salary structure with profit-based bonuses but no payout rate or grid. Merrill describes its incentive award program and a growth-based reduction rule tied to an incentive compensation grid, but no payout percentages. Schwab describes broad compensation components (base pay, incentive pay, equity) and a retirement career achievement plan but no advisor payout grid or rate. These disclosures are not directly comparable across firms because the definitions, units, scopes, and periods differ (some firms disclose percentage payout rates, others only structural descriptions or deferred-compensation mixes), so they cannot be ranked on a single common basis.

adjacent.text: Edward Jones: The nearest disclosure to a payout rate is that financial advisors are generally compensated on commission, subject to a minimum guaranteed salary, with additional compensation based on branch and Partnership profitability; most advisors receive a discretionary portion of the Program Fee; and a portion of brokerage sales charges or commissions is paid to the advisor, who typically earns more upfront on brokerage but more over time on Advisory Solutions Fund Models.
adjacent.differs_because: The passages describe Edward Jones' general advisor compensation structure (commission basis with a minimum guaranteed salary, additional compensation tied to branch and Partnership profitability, and a discretionary share of the Program Fee), but do not disclose a specific payout grid or payout rate.

adjacent.text: Merrill: The nearest disclosure to a payout grid is that advisors are eligible for a compensation award, payable over a defined period, from an incentive program based on prior-year growth targets in new households and assets/liabilities, and that an advisor faces a reduction in their incentive compensation grid if they fail to achieve growth in the assets and liabilities component for two consecutive years.
adjacent.differs_because: Merrill describes the structure of its advisor incentive compensation award and the existence of an incentive compensation grid (growth-target-based, with a reduction for two consecutive years of missed growth in assets and liabilities), but it does not disclose an actual payout grid or payout rate (no payout percentages or rate schedule).

adjacent.text: The Charles Schwab Corporation: The nearest disclosure to a change in advisor compensation is that its Schwab Wealth Advisory brochure was revised since June 2026 to reflect updates to the compensation arrangement between CS&Co. and sponsors/issuers of certain third-party exchange-traded products for platform services provided by CS&Co., with a Notice of Change also noting removal of the Schwab Guided Portfolios (SGP) Custom option (no longer offered).
adjacent.differs_because: The disclosed change concerns CS&Co.'s own compensation received from third-party ETF sponsors/issuers for platform services (firm revenue), not how Schwab's financial consultants or wealth advisors are compensated.

gaps.what: Raymond James reports non-qualified deferred compensation plans providing returns based on referenced investments, and annual recruitment/retention award amortization, but the advisor payout grid detail (other than the affiliation-model payout ranges) remains at firm-level and model-level disclosure rather than a full per-advisor rate schedule.
gaps.suggested_source: Firm recruiting/affiliation-options pages and ADV; full internal payout schedules are not published
